report.summary: A data project compares advertised pay rates for people training AI, flagging single-source claims and correcting unsupported figures rather than treating them as guaranteed wages.
report.background: Modern AI models, especially large language models, depend on human workers who label data, rank responses, write prompts, and provide feedback. Much of this work is mediated by global platforms that advertise hourly or per-task rates to attract contributors. Those advertised numbers often differ from actual earnings because of task scarcity, unpaid onboarding, rejected work, location-based pay, and payment thresholds. The site documents this gap by compiling rate bands from first-party listings, third-party guides, and individual claims. It treats highlighted single-source rows as claims rather than facts, and it names and dates every source. When sources disagree, it prints both rather than averaging. The project has issued seven corrections, including removing unsupported bands and replacing payout records that platforms contradicted. This reflects a broader push for transparency in AI supply chains, where labor conditions are often obscured by layers of contractors and vendors.
key_points: Advertised rates are not guaranteed wages. The project explicitly labels its bands as the lowest and highest advertised figures, not take-home pay. Actual earnings can fall below the advertised ceiling due to task availability, unpaid training, rejected submissions, and regional pay differences. Readers should treat the numbers as marketing signals, not verified compensation.

Every pay band carries an evidence class. A figure can come from a first-party listing, two agreeing guides, or a single source marked as a claim rather than a fact. Highlighted rows signal that only one source supports the band, so the number is provisional. This grading system helps users judge how much confidence to place in each rate.

Disagreements are preserved, not averaged. Where sources conflict, the project prints both figures and refuses to blend them into a false midpoint. This is important because averaging conflicting pay data can hide important differences between platforms, regions, and worker categories. It also makes the underlying uncertainty visible to researchers, journalists, and workers.

Corrections are public and substantive. Seven corrections have been published, including one that removed three unsupported bands and another that replaced payout records contradicted by platforms' own pages. A public corrections log increases accountability and shows the dataset is maintained rather than static. It also warns readers that early or single-source numbers may later be revised or retracted.

The method page names and dates every source. This allows independent checking and replication. It also distinguishes the project from anonymous wage crowdsourcing, where provenance is often unclear. For workers, it offers a way to compare advertised promises against documented evidence; for platforms, it creates pressure to publish clearer, verifiable pay information.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this kind of comparison exposes a hidden cost center: human data labor. Companies that rely on annotation and RLHF vendors may face questions about fair pay, supply-chain transparency, and reputational risk. Developers and AI startups should treat advertised rates as a starting point for due diligence, not as proof of ethical sourcing. They may need to audit vendors, budget for higher real wages, and document worker treatment. For regular users, the report demystifies how chatbots and generative models are trained, showing that AI often depends on precarious human labor. It may also empower workers to negotiate, compare platforms, or avoid misleading gig ads. Regulators and researchers can use the evidence-grading method to demand better disclosures.
report.tools: To follow up, watch the project's comparison, method, and corrections pages at blastradius.dpdns.org. Useful complementary tools include the Wayback Machine for archiving changing payout pages, Fairwork's platform ratings, Rest of World and Bloomberg's gig-labor reporting, and open-source datasets like Data Workers' Inquiry. For developers, vendor audits and worker surveys can help verify advertised rates. Track platform payout pages directly, and use spreadsheets or Airtable to log dated screenshots, as the site does.
